subtopics.title: Properties and structure of the three states

outcomes.text: State the distinguishing properties of solids, liquids and gases.
Describe how particles are separated, arranged and moving in each state.

subtopics.title: Changes of state and gas behaviour

outcomes.text: Describe melting, boiling, evaporating, freezing and condensing.
Describe how temperature and pressure change the volume of a gas.
Explain changes of state with kinetic particle theory, including heating and cooling curves.
Explain the effect of temperature and pressure on gas volume using kinetic particle theory.
Describe and explain diffusion using kinetic particle theory.
Describe and explain how relative molecular mass changes the rate of diffusion of gases.
Describe the differences between elements, compounds and mixtures.

topics.title: 2.2 Atomic structure and the Periodic Table

outcomes.text: Describe the atom as a nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons in shells.
State the relative charges and masses of protons, neutrons and electrons.
Define proton (atomic) number.
Define mass (nucleon) number.

subtopics.title: Electronic configuration and the Periodic Table

outcomes.text: Work out electronic configurations of atoms and ions with proton number 1 to 20.
Link full outer shells, outer electrons and shell count to noble gases, group and period.
Define isotopes as atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons.
Interpret and use symbols for atoms and ions.
Explain why isotopes of an element share chemical properties.
Calculate relative atomic mass from isotope masses and abundances.
Describe how cations and anions form.
State that an ionic bond is a strong attraction between oppositely charged ions.
Describe ionic bonding between Group I and Group VII elements with dot-and-cross diagrams.
Describe ionic bonding between metal and non-metal ions with dot-and-cross diagrams.
Describe the giant lattice of alternating positive and negative ions.
Describe the properties of ionic compounds: high melting and boiling points, and conductivity when molten or aqueous.
Explain these properties using structure and bonding.
State that a covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons giving noble gas configurations.
Describe covalent bonding in H2, Cl2, H2O, CH4, NH3 and HCl with dot-and-cross diagrams.
Describe covalent bonding in CH3OH, C2H4, O2, CO2 and N2 with dot-and-cross diagrams.
Describe the low melting points, low boiling points and poor conductivity of simple molecular compounds.
Explain these properties using weak intermolecular forces and structure.
Describe the giant covalent structures of graphite and diamond.
Relate the structures of graphite and diamond to uses as lubricant, electrode and cutting tool.
Describe the giant structure of silicon(IV) oxide.
Describe the similarity in properties of diamond and silicon(IV) oxide, from structure.
Describe metallic bonding as attraction between positive ions and a sea of delocalised electrons.
Explain good conductivity, malleability and ductility of metals from structure and bonding.
State the formulae of the elements and compounds named in the content.
Define the molecular formula of a compound.
Deduce the formula of a simple compound from a model or diagram.
Construct word equations and symbol equations with state symbols.
Define the empirical formula of a compound.
Deduce the formula of an ionic compound from ion numbers or charges.
Construct symbol equations with state symbols, including ionic equations.
Deduce a full symbol equation from information given.

topics.title: 3.2 Relative masses of atoms and molecules

outcomes.text: Describe relative atomic mass as the average mass of an element's isotopes compared to 1/12 of carbon-12.
Define relative molecular (formula) mass as the sum of relative atomic masses.
Calculate reacting masses in simple proportions, without the mole.

topics.title: 3.3 The mole and the Avogadro constant

outcomes.text: State that a mole is the unit of amount of substance and holds 6.02 x 10^23 particles.
Use amount = mass / molar mass to find amount, mass, molar mass, relative mass or number of particles.
Use the molar gas volume of 24 dm3 at r.t.p. in gas calculations.
State that concentration is measured in g/dm3 or mol/dm3.
Calculate reacting masses, limiting reactants, gas volumes and solution volumes and concentrations, converting cm3 and dm3.
Use titration data to find moles of solute, concentration or volume.
Calculate empirical and molecular formulae from data.
Calculate percentage yield, percentage composition by mass and percentage purity.
Define electrolysis as breaking down a molten or aqueous ionic compound with electric current.
Identify the anode, cathode and electrolyte in a simple cell.
Describe charge transfer: electron movement in the wire, electron loss or gain at electrodes, ion movement in the electrolyte.
Identify products and observations for molten lead(II) bromide, concentrated aqueous sodium chloride and dilute sulfuric acid.
State that metals or hydrogen form at the cathode and non-metals at the anode.
Predict products for a molten binary compound.
Identify products for aqueous copper(II) sulfate with carbon and with copper electrodes.
Predict products for halide compounds in dilute or concentrated solution.
Write ionic half-equations for oxidation at the anode and reduction at the cathode.
State that electroplating improves appearance and resists corrosion.
Describe how metals are electroplated.
State that a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell makes electricity with water as the only product.
Describe advantages and disadvantages of fuel cells compared with petrol engines.
State that exothermic reactions give heat to the surroundings and raise their temperature.
State that endothermic reactions take in heat and lower the temperature of the surroundings.
Interpret reaction pathway diagrams for both types.
State that the enthalpy change, delta H, is negative for exothermic and positive for endothermic reactions.
Define activation energy as the minimum energy colliding particles need to react.
Draw and label reaction pathway diagrams showing reactants, products, delta H and activation energy.
Explain enthalpy change using bond breaking (endothermic) and bond making (exothermic).
Calculate the enthalpy change of a reaction from bond energies.
Identify physical and chemical changes and describe how they differ.
Describe how concentration, pressure, surface area, temperature and catalysts affect rate.
State that a catalyst speeds up a reaction and is unchanged at the end.
Describe collision theory: particles per unit volume, collision frequency, kinetic energy and activation energy.
Explain each rate factor using collision theory.
State that a catalyst lowers the activation energy.
Describe practical methods for rates, such as mass change and gas formation.
Interpret data and graphs from rate experiments.
Evaluate practical methods for investigating rate.
State that some reactions are reversible, shown by the symbol for reversibility.
Describe how heat and water change hydrated copper(II) sulfate and cobalt(II) chloride.
State that equilibrium in a closed system has equal forward and reverse rates and constant concentrations.
Predict and explain how temperature, pressure, concentration and catalyst affect the position of equilibrium.
State the symbol equation for making ammonia.
State the sources of hydrogen (methane) and nitrogen (air).
State the typical conditions: 450 C, 200 atm and an iron catalyst.
State the symbol equation for converting sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide.
State the sources of sulfur dioxide and oxygen.
State the typical conditions: 450 C, 2 atm and vanadium(V) oxide.
Explain the conditions in both processes using rate, equilibrium, safety and economics.

subtopics.title: Oxidation and reduction as oxygen change

outcomes.text: Use a Roman numeral to show the oxidation number of an element in a compound.
Define redox as simultaneous oxidation and reduction.
Define oxidation as gain of oxygen and reduction as loss of oxygen.
Identify redox reactions by oxygen gain and loss.
Identify oxidation and reduction in redox reactions.

subtopics.title: Redox in terms of electrons and oxidation numbers

outcomes.text: Define oxidation as loss of electrons or increased oxidation number.
Define reduction as gain of electrons or decreased oxidation number.
Identify redox reactions by electron gain and loss.
Identify redox by changes in oxidation number using the rules for elements, ions and compounds.
Identify redox from colour changes with acidified potassium manganate(VII) or potassium iodide.
Define an oxidising agent.
Define a reducing agent.
Identify oxidising and reducing agents in redox reactions.

topics.title: 7.1 The characteristic properties of acids and bases

outcomes.text: Describe acid reactions with metals, bases and carbonates.
Describe the effect of acids on litmus, thymolphthalein and methyl orange.
State that acids in water contain H+ ions.
State that bases are metal oxides or hydroxides and alkalis are soluble bases.
Describe base reactions with acids and ammonium salts.
Describe the effect of alkalis on litmus, thymolphthalein and methyl orange.
State that alkaline solutions contain OH- ions.
Compare acidity, neutrality and alkalinity by colour and pH using universal indicator paper.
Describe neutralisation: H+ and OH- make water.
Define acids as proton donors and bases as proton acceptors.
Define strong and weak acids by complete or partial dissociation.
State that hydrochloric acid is strong and show it by equation.
State that ethanoic acid is weak and show it by equation.
Classify oxides as acidic (SO2, CO2) or basic (CuO, CaO) by metallic character.
Describe amphoteric oxides as reacting with both acids and bases.
Classify Al2O3 and ZnO as amphoteric.
Describe preparing and purifying soluble salts from an acid with an alkali, metal, insoluble base or carbonate.
Describe the general solubility rules for sodium, potassium, ammonium, nitrate, chloride, sulfate, carbonate and hydroxide salts.
Describe preparing insoluble salts by precipitation.
Define hydrated and anhydrous substances.
Define water of crystallisation, including CuSO4.5H2O and CoCl2.6H2O.
Describe the table as periods and groups in order of proton number.
Describe the change from metallic to non-metallic character across a period.
Describe how group number relates to ion charge.
Explain similar chemistry within a group using electronic configuration.
Explain how an element's position predicts its properties.
Identify group trends from given information.
Describe lithium, sodium and potassium as soft metals with falling melting point, rising density and rising reactivity.
Predict properties of other Group I elements from given data.
Describe chlorine, bromine and iodine as diatomic non-metals with rising density and falling reactivity down the group.
State the appearance of the halogens at r.t.p.
Describe and explain halogen displacement reactions with halide ions.
Predict properties of other Group VII elements from given data.
Describe transition elements as dense, high-melting, coloured-compound-forming metals and often catalysts.
Describe their ions as having variable oxidation numbers, such as iron(II) and iron(III).
Describe noble gases as unreactive monatomic gases and explain this from electronic configuration.
Compare metals and non-metals for conductivity, malleability, ductility and melting and boiling points.
Describe metal reactions with dilute acids, cold water and steam, and oxygen.
Describe metal uses from physical properties, such as aluminium in aircraft, cables and food containers, and copper in wiring.
Describe an alloy as a mixture of a metal with other elements, such as brass and stainless steel.
State that alloys can be harder and stronger than pure metals.
Describe uses of alloys, such as stainless steel cutlery.
Identify alloys from structure diagrams.
Explain why alloys are harder: different-sized atoms stop layers sliding.
State the order of the reactivity series.
Describe reactions of metals with cold water, steam and dilute hydrochloric acid and explain them using the series.
Deduce a reactivity order from experimental results.
Describe reactivity as tendency to form positive ions, using displacement reactions with metal ions.
Explain the apparent unreactivity of aluminium by its oxide layer.
State the conditions needed for iron and steel to rust.
State barrier methods such as painting, greasing and plastic coating.
Describe how barrier methods exclude oxygen or water.
Describe zinc galvanising as both barrier and sacrificial protection.
Explain sacrificial protection using the reactivity series and electron loss.
Describe how ease of extraction relates to position in the reactivity series.
Describe the blast furnace: burning coke, forming CO, reducing iron(III) oxide, decomposing limestone and forming slag.
State the symbol equations for extracting iron from hematite.
State that bauxite is the main aluminium ore and aluminium is extracted by electrolysis.
Describe aluminium extraction: role of cryolite, replacing carbon anodes and electrode reactions with half-equations.
Describe tests for water with anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride and copper(II) sulfate.
Describe testing water purity with melting and boiling points.
Explain why distilled water is used in practicals.
State substances that natural water may contain, including oxygen, metal compounds, plastics, sewage, microbes, nitrates and phosphates.
State which of these are beneficial.
State which are harmful and why.
Describe domestic water treatment: sedimentation, filtration, carbon and chlorination.
State that ammonium salts and nitrates are fertilisers.
Describe NPK fertilisers providing nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
State the composition of clean dry air.
State the sources of carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, particulates, methane, nitrogen oxides and sulfur dioxide.
State the adverse effects of each pollutant.
Describe how carbon dioxide and methane cause global warming by absorbing, reflecting and emitting thermal energy.
State strategies against climate change: planting trees, less livestock farming, less fossil fuel, more hydrogen and renewables.
State strategies against acid rain: catalytic converters, low-sulfur fuels and flue gas desulfurisation with calcium oxide.
Explain how nitrogen oxides form in car engines and how catalytic converters remove them.
Describe photosynthesis as carbon dioxide and water making glucose and oxygen with chlorophyll and light.
State the word equation for photosynthesis.
State the symbol equation for photosynthesis.
Draw and interpret displayed formulae.
Write general formulae for alkanes, alkenes, alcohols and carboxylic acids.
Identify a functional group.
State that a structural formula unambiguously shows how atoms are arranged.
Define structural isomers, e.g. the isomers of C4H10 and C4H8.
State that a homologous series has the same functional group and similar chemistry.
Describe a homologous series: same functional group and general formula, CH2 steps, physical trends, similar chemistry.
State what saturated compounds are.
State what unsaturated compounds are.
Name and draw methane, ethane, ethene, ethanol, ethanoic acid and products of reactions in 11.4 to 11.7.
State the compound type from a name ending in -ane, -ene, -ol or -oic acid, or from a formula.
Name and draw structural and displayed formulae of unbranched alkanes, alkenes, alcohols and carboxylic acids up to four carbons.
Name and draw unbranched esters from alcohols and carboxylic acids of up to four carbons.
Name coal, natural gas and petroleum as fossil fuels.
Name methane as the main constituent of natural gas.
State that hydrocarbons contain only hydrogen and carbon.
State that petroleum is a mixture of hydrocarbons.

subtopics.title: Fractional distillation and uses of fractions

outcomes.text: Describe separating petroleum by fractional distillation.
Describe how fraction properties change up the column: shorter chains, more volatile, lower boiling point, less viscous.
Name the uses of the fractions, from refinery gas to bitumen.
State that alkanes have single covalent bonds and are saturated hydrocarbons.
Describe alkanes as generally unreactive apart from combustion and chlorine substitution.
State what a substitution reaction is.
Describe alkane substitution with chlorine as a photochemical reaction with UV light and draw monosubstituted products.
State that alkenes have a carbon-carbon double bond and are unsaturated.
Describe making alkenes and hydrogen by cracking larger alkanes with heat and a catalyst.
Describe the reasons for cracking.
Describe the bromine water test for saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons.
State that an addition reaction forms only one product.
Describe alkene addition with bromine, hydrogen and nickel, and steam with acid, and draw the products.
Describe making ethanol by fermentation of glucose with yeast at 25 to 35 C without oxygen.
Describe making ethanol by adding steam to ethene at 300 C and 60 atm with an acid catalyst.
Weigh the advantages and disadvantages of the two methods.
Describe the combustion of ethanol.
State the uses of ethanol as a solvent and a fuel.
Describe ethanoic acid reacting with metals, bases and carbonates, naming the salts.
Describe making ethanoic acid by oxidising ethanol with potassium manganate(VII) or bacteria in vinegar making.
Describe a carboxylic acid and an alcohol forming an ester with an acid catalyst.
Define polymers as large molecules made from monomers.
Describe poly(ethene) forming by addition polymerisation of ethene.
Deduce an addition polymer's structure or repeat unit from its alkene, and vice versa.
Deduce a condensation polymer's structure from its monomers, and vice versa: polyamides and polyesters.
Identify repeat units and linkages in addition and condensation polymers.
Describe the differences between addition and condensation polymerisation.
Describe and draw the structures of nylon and PET.
State that plastics are made from polymers.
Describe how plastic properties affect their disposal.
Describe environmental challenges: landfill, ocean build-up and toxic fumes from burning.
State that PET can be converted back into monomers and re-polymerised.
Describe proteins as natural polyamides made from amino acids with different side chains.
Describe and draw the structure of proteins.
Name apparatus for time, temperature, mass and volume.
Suggest advantages and disadvantages of methods and apparatus.
Describe solvent, solute, solution, saturated solution, residue and filtrate.
Describe an acid-base titration with a burette, volumetric pipette and indicator.
Describe how an indicator shows the end-point.
Describe paper chromatography for separating soluble coloured mixtures.
Interpret chromatograms to identify unknowns and pure or impure substances.
Describe chromatography of colourless substances using a locating agent.
State and use the equation for Rf.
Describe and explain separation using solvents, filtration, crystallisation, simple and fractional distillation.
Suggest suitable techniques for given substances.
Identify substances and assess purity using melting and boiling points.
Describe the test for carbonate.
Describe tests for chloride, bromide and iodide.
Describe the test for nitrate.
Describe tests for sulfate and sulfite.
Describe tests for cations using sodium hydroxide and ammonia: Al, NH4, Ca, Cr, Cu, Fe(II), Fe(III) and Zn.
Describe flame tests for lithium, sodium, potassium, calcium, barium and copper.
Describe tests for ammonia, carbon dioxide, chlorine, hydrogen, oxygen and sulfur dioxide.
